questions.question: When will quantum computers actually be useful?

hybrid.answer:
Quantum computers are already starting to be useful, and the real transformational impact is due this decade, by 2030. At IBM, our roadmap says the first provable quantum advantage comes in 2026, and the first fault-tolerant machine comes by 2030 [1][2].

**Today:** Today's machines aren't error corrected, but errors can be mitigated. The scaling is still exponential, but it is a slower exponential, so you can already get value with current architectures [3]. What we can do now is start simulating small molecules [4]. Error rates have improved a lot: our latest Heron processor has a two-qubit error of 5 to 10 to the minus 4, which allows calculations with thousands of gate operations, up to the 5,000 to 10,000 range [5].

**Next step (2026):** At IBM, we expect the first real quantum advantage, meaning a real application on a real system that classical computing alone cannot do [6]. Early examples will probably be chemistry and catalysis [7]. In finance, HSBC reported a 34% better accuracy in predicting the probability that a trade order gets filled at a given price, though there is no proof yet that a classical computer couldn't do this [8].

**By 2030:** At IBM, we plan the first fault-tolerant machine, which implements universal quantum computing and brings the transformational impact [2]. Our roadmap goes toward 100,000 and then 1 million error-corrected qubits [9].

**Where it matters most:** The biggest impact should come in simulating nature (chemistry, biology, materials), in global optimization, and in finding hidden structure in small but complex data sets [10].

One related point: once machines reach that level, today's public-key cryptography will be attacked and stop working, and I think we are already late in preparing for that [11].

questions.question: Should banks be worried about quantum computers breaking encryption?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, and the time to act is now. In my view we are already late. [1]

**Why it matters:**
- At IBM, our roadmap points to a provable quantum advantage on some application by next year (said in 2025) and the first fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2030. [2]
- At that point, asymmetric (public-key) cryptography will be attacked and no longer work. That covers secure internet connections, digital signatures and secure data transmission, and also secure digital currency such as a future digital euro. [3]

**Why waiting is a mistake:**
- Solutions to move to something secure against quantum attacks already exist, but one has to start now rather than wait and hope the threat is 30 years away. [1]
- Someone is already collecting encrypted data that circulates on the internet and storing it. Once quantum computers are available, that person can go back, read the data and even forge digital signatures and contracts. [4]

**What I recommend:**
- Move toward quantum-safe algorithms, and build in crypto agility so you can migrate from one cryptography to another easily. Nobody can guarantee that today's quantum-safe algorithms will stay secure forever, because cryptography by definition is not secure forever. [5]

questions.question: What about the energy cost of all this AI?

hybrid.answer:
My view is that the energy problem depends on how you build the models, and that the smarter route cuts energy by a large margin.

**Two ways to evolve the field.** One is a single model that integrates all the data and all the modalities. That could bring many discoveries by connecting data from different environments, but it would be hugely expensive, especially in use, since a model is trained once but used a million times [1]. A model with 1,000 trillion parameters makes no sense for a trivial question like where to go to dinner [1].

**Why scale matters.** The energy needed to train a model doesn't scale linearly with model size; it scales at least quadratically [1].

**What I prefer.** Instead of one giant model, build around 100 models of roughly 1 to 10 trillion parameters each, specialized in tasks, modalities or use cases. An orchestrator on top, which can itself be an AI model, as in agentic AI, calls the individual models and integrates their answers [2]. Because of the quadratic scaling, the sum of the smaller models is much cheaper than the full one, so done right you can get results with an order of magnitude less energy and also more accurate [2].

**Accuracy benefit.** Mixing too many uncorrelated things can make a model give nonsensical answers, because it only learns sequences and predicts the next step [3]. Specialized models help avoid that.

**Avoiding duplicated effort.** I also push for building base models openly and collaboratively, once, in a pre-competitive way. Otherwise people redo the same models with lots of compute power and CO2 emissions to get the same result [4].
